clinicalPearls: Caused by loss-of-function variants in ANK2, which encodes ankyrin-B, a cytoskeletal adaptor that anchors ion channels and transporters in cardiomyocytes.
Originally labelled long QT syndrome type 4 (LQT4), but QT prolongation is inconsistent, so it is better regarded as a distinct 'ankyrin-B syndrome'.
The characteristic phenotype is a mixed arrhythmia picture: sinus node dysfunction with bradycardia, atrial fibrillation and susceptibility to ventricular arrhythmia.
Catecholamine- and exercise-induced ventricular tachycardia can resemble CPVT and may cause syncope or sudden cardiac death.
Penetrance and expressivity are highly variable, even within a single family carrying the same variant.
It is fundamentally a disorder of membrane protein organisation rather than a classic single ion-channel channelopathy.
The resting ECG may be normal or show only borderline QT changes, so provocation testing and prolonged monitoring are often required.
reference.pathophysiology: Ankyrin-B, encoded by ANK2, is a large adaptor protein that links integral membrane proteins to the underlying spectrin-based cytoskeleton, organising functional microdomains within cardiomyocytes. It is required for the correct localisation and stability of the sodium–potassium ATPase, the sodium–calcium exchanger and the inositol trisphosphate receptor at the transverse-tubule and sarcoplasmic-reticulum junction. Loss-of-function ANK2 variants cause mislocalisation and reduced expression of these transporters, disturbing intracellular sodium and calcium handling. The resulting calcium-handling abnormality promotes afterdepolarisations and triggered activity, particularly under adrenergic stress, while disordered ion transport in nodal and atrial tissue produces sinus node dysfunction and atrial arrhythmia. Because the defect lies in membrane protein targeting rather than in a single channel's gating, the electrophysiological phenotype is broad and the QT interval is only variably prolonged, distinguishing it from the canonical long QT channelopathies.
additionalDifferentials: Congenital long QT syndrome types 1–3 (KCNQ1, KCNH2, SCN5A)
Sinus node dysfunction or sick sinus syndrome of other cause
Acquired QT prolongation from drugs or electrolyte disturbance
additionalInvestigations: 12-lead ECG with serial and exercise/recovery assessment of the QT interval
Ambulatory Holter and prolonged or implantable rhythm monitoring for bradycardia, atrial fibrillation and ventricular ectopy
Exercise stress testing to unmask catecholamine-provoked ventricular arrhythmia
ANK2 genetic testing within an inherited-arrhythmia gene panel, with cascade family screening
Echocardiography to exclude structural heart disease
Electrolyte and thyroid assessment to exclude reversible causes of arrhythmia
Family history review and clinical evaluation of first-degree relatives
redFlags: Exertional or stress-induced syncope, which may herald malignant ventricular arrhythmia
Documented polymorphic ventricular tachycardia or an aborted cardiac arrest
Family history of unexplained sudden cardiac death, especially at a young age
Profound symptomatic bradycardia or prolonged sinus pauses
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is variable and genotype–phenotype correlations are weak; many carriers remain relatively asymptomatic, but sinus node dysfunction, atrial fibrillation and life-threatening ventricular arrhythmia can occur and sudden cardiac death is described. Risk-directed monitoring and avoidance of arrhythmia triggers underpin management.
pitfalls: Excluding the diagnosis because the QT interval is normal, when QT prolongation is inconsistent in ankyrin-B syndrome.
Managing it as classic long QT syndrome types 1–3 and overlooking the prominent sinus node dysfunction and atrial fibrillation.
Missing exercise-induced ventricular arrhythmia by relying on a resting ECG alone.
Failing to screen first-degree relatives given the variable and incompletely penetrant phenotype.
management: Avoid arrhythmia triggers by withdrawing QT-prolonging drugs and correcting electrolyte disturbances
Use beta-blockade to blunt catecholamine- and exercise-induced ventricular arrhythmia
Implant a permanent pacemaker for symptomatic sinus node dysfunction and bradycardia
Consider an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator in those with life-threatening ventricular arrhythmia or aborted sudden cardiac death
Manage atrial fibrillation with rate or rhythm control and assess thromboembolic risk for anticoagulation
Advise restriction of competitive and strenuous exertion, and provide risk-directed rhythm monitoring under a specialist inherited-arrhythmia service
Offer ANK2 genetic testing, genetic counselling, and cascade family screening
